extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of The Spectator; readers interested in morals, conduct, and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical/essayistic guidance on judging and portraying moral qualities, social conduct, and taste — the sort of moralizing reflections found in early-18th-century Spectator essays. Useful for writers crafting character sketches or moral commentary in short essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: True modesty vs. false modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: True Modesty is ashamed to do anything that is repugnant to the Rules of right Reason: False Modesty is ashamed to do anything that is opposite to the Humour of the Company. True Modesty avoids everything that is criminal, false Modesty everything that is unfashionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to judge characters and conduct: true modesty is principled, limited by prudence and religion; false modesty is an undetermined instinct that seeks to gratify others rather than self and often betrays virtue. (Includes the summed contrast: 'The one guards Virtue, the other betrays it.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty that compels vice or restrains good is vicious
rubrics_metrics.description: We may conclude that Modesty to be false and vicious, which engages a Man to do any thing that is ill or indiscreet, or which restrains him from doing any thing that is of a contrary Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative anti-patterns: lending sums you cannot spare, becoming surety for people you barely know, giving recommendatory characters for strangers, bestowing places on those you don't esteem, living contrary to your own sense — all 'meerly because they have not the Confidence to resist Solicitation, Importunity or Example.' Use such behaviours as symptoms of false modesty in character depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: False modesty exposes to criminal actions and social contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man of vicious Modesty complies with everything, and is only fearful of doing what may look singular in the Company where he is engaged. He falls in with the Torrent, and lets himself go to every Action or Discourse, however unjustifiable in itself, so it be in Vogue among the present Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character-rule: false modesty produces conformity even to immoral acts; use examples like unwilling gamblers or those who commit wrongs to avoid singularity. Quote/appeal to Xenophanes: 'I confess that I am exceeding timorous, for I dare not do any ill thing' as model of true courage by refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sincere virtue visible to hypocrisy or open impiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypocrisie cannot indeed be too much detested, but at the same time is to be preferred to open Impiety. ... The due Mean to be observed is to be sincerely Virtuous, and at the same time to let the World see we are so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value characters who are both genuinely virtuous and not ashamed to show it; the public display of virtue matters to social health. Use the moral judgment that secrecy of goodness (perverted modesty) is condemned in Scripture and social ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality (practice) has pre-eminence over Faith (belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion may be considered under two heads: Faith (what we are to believe) and Morality (what we are to practise). The first has the pre-eminence in several respects, but overall morality is of a fixed eternal nature and often more certain and beneficial in practical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing characters or doctrines, emphasise the social and psychological benefits of morality: it endures when faith fails; it can do greater worldly good; it quiets the mind and moderates the passions; there is wider civil agreement on moral points. Use the six enumerated reasons as criteria for preferring moral conduct in character assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith's excellency lies in how it strengthens and enforces morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith seems to draw its principal, if not all its excellency, from the Influence it has upon Morality; ... In explaining and carrying to greater Heights several Points of Morality; In furnishing new and stronger Motives to enforce the Practice of Morality; In giving more amiable Ideas of the Supreme Being; By shewing the Blackness and Deformity of Vice; In being the ordinary method of making Morality effectual to Salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use faith in narratives as valuable primarily where it amplifies moral behaviour and motive. Avoid treating doctrinal belief as valuable in isolation from its moral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Don’t endorse any article of faith that weakens practical morality
rubrics_metrics.description: That we should be particularly cautious of making any thing an Article of Faith, which does not contribute to the Confirmation or Improvement of Morality. That no Article of Faith can be true and authentick, which weakens or subverts the practical part of Religion, or what I have hitherto called Morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative rule for belief or ideology within a story or essay: test doctrines by their likely social consequences. Use the prosecuting-conscience example to dramatise the harms that follow from doctrines that sanction persecuting others.

rubrics_metrics.name: In doubtful principles, consider the harmful consequences if they prove erroneous
rubrics_metrics.description: We should, in all dubious Points, consider any ill Consequences that may arise from them, supposing they should be Erroneous, before we give up our Assent to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a prudential test: if adherence to a belief would cause grievous harm (imprisonment, ruin, hatred, death) then require near-certainty before endorsing it. Useful device for character conflict and moral dilemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper decorum in sacred assemblies: worship, not social display
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies, Bows, Courtesies, Whisperings, Smiles, Winks, Nods, with other familiar Arts of Salutation, which take up in our Churches so much Time, that might be better employed, and which seem so utterly inconsistent with the Duty and true Intent of our entering into those Religious Assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe church behaviour that favours solemn attention over social observance; suggest foreign examples (Roman Catholic or Muslim conventions of seeming unknowing to keep minds engaged) as models. Use tension between social ritual and genuine devotion as material for scenes and moral critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry in company: social charm excuses faults but can mask vice
rubrics_metrics.description: People are not aware of the very great Force which Pleasantry in Company has upon all those with whom a Man of that Talent converses. His Faults are generally overlooked ... When this Quality is conspicuous in a Man who has, to accompany it, manly and virtuous Sentiments, there cannot certainly be any thing which can give so pleasing Gratification; but when it is alone, and serves only to gild a Crowd of ill Qualities, there is no Man so much to be avoided as your pleasant Fellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character rule: pleasantness is a social lubricant that can excuse or conceal faults; dramatise the moral hazard when charm replaces conscience. Examples: Dacinthus forgiven broken promises; a pleasant person may debauch and harm yet remain welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity, Self-Conceit, and Opinion as social seductions to folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory: Vanity enthroned with Self-Conceit as Cupid, supported by Flattery, Affectation, and Fashion; Opinion and Error bewitch crowds into the Palace of Vanity, whose splendor lacks real foundation and collapses into shame, poverty, or contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the allegory's elements as criteria to diagnose characters: watch for the roles of flattery (colouring), affectation (airs), fashion (concealing defects). Plot device: the eventual fall of vanity reveals true worth and reorders esteem; plain-dealing is at first slighted but may eventually expose the delusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery, Affectation, and Fashion function to secure esteem and hide defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattery gave new Colours and Complections to all Things. Affectation new Airs and Appearances, which, as she said, were not vulgar, and Fashion both concealed some home Defects, and added some foreign external Beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters of rank or social performers, attribute specific social technologies to sustain vanity: flattering speech, borrowed airs, ever-changing fashions. These are tools that help characters maintain false esteem and are useful markers of inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride: ubiquitous passion that can be virtuous or dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one Passion which all Mankind so naturally give into as Pride, nor any other Passion which appears in such different Disguises: It is to be found in all Habits and all Complexions. ... Is it not a Question whether it does more Harm or Good in the World? And if there be not such a Thing as what we may call a virtuous and laudable Pride?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pride as a complex motive in characterization: it opens people to flatterers and can be politically useful (example of Charles II's affability winning public favour), but when misapplied it exposes individuals and polities to manipulation. Use concrete anecdotes (the King taking another bottle with the mayor) to show how personal gaiety can have public consequences.
